📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sponsored by Eli Lilly and Organization.

One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.

Recent findings suggest that at its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell. It also includes cognitive health—your ability to think, learn, and remember.

According to recent reports, because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it. Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease can begin about 20 years before symptoms appear, making a proactive approach to brain health an important part of caring for your overall health.

Recent findings suggest that this messaging inspired actress, author, and advocate Julianne Moore to partner with Eli Lilly and Organization on their Brain Health Matters campaign to encourage people to prioritize their brain health. “From my conversations with people living with Alzheimer’s disease, I’ve seen how much proactive care matters,” Moore says. “That’s why I’m helping to encourage everyone to prioritize their brain health through regular conversations with their doctors.”.

Not sure where to begin? Here are five ways to make brain health a priority part in your overall health.

You might not have any concerns about cognitive decline, much less dementia. But taking a proactive approach to cognitive health doesn’t have to wait until later in life—or until something feels off. One brain change associated with Alzheimer’s disease involves amyloid, a protein the body produces naturally. Talking to your doctor can help you understand your personal risk factors and discuss whether steps such as establishing a cognitive baseline and adopting brain-healthy habits may be appropriate for you.

Add brain health to your “must-ask” list for medical appointments and come prepared with specific questions to guide the conversation. Ask your doctor whether a cognitive assessment is appropriate for you. This spoken, written, or digital evaluation can provide a starting point for monitoring your memory and thinking over time.

While a cognitive assessment cannot diagnose a condition on its own, establishing a baseline and completing follow-up assessments as recommended by your doctor may help spot early signs of memory and thinking problems and monitor changes over time.

Here’s what you may want to ask your doctor:.

Sources indicate that research shows that up to 45 percent of dementia cases, including those caused by Alzheimer’s disease, may be prevented or delayed by managing changeable risk factors. These include blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; lifestyle habits around diet, exercise, alcohol consumption, and smoking; and even hearing loss, depression, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and sleep.

You can’t change everything that affects your risk—such as age, family history, or certain genetic markers. But your doctor can help you understand the risk factors that may apply to you and build a proposal to manage those that can be changed. The following brain-healthy habits can be a good place to start:.

Once you understand your risk factors, establish a cognitive baseline, and identify brain-healthy habits that could work for you, the next step is bringing those pieces together. Work with your doctor to create a strategy based on your individual health needs.

Your plan might include ways to manage changeable risk factors, behaviors that support your brain health, and a schedule for revisiting your cognitive health with your doctor. Regular conversations with your doctor about these topics can help you take action early and help support your brain health for the future.

Industry observers note that honest discussions around brain health can help go a long way toward reducing stigma and helping others feel more comfortable seeking information, support, and care. Opening up—even in small ways—can make a difference, whether you’re checking in with loved ones, sharing your own concerns, or simply normalizing the topic in everyday life.

Sources indicate that “Brain health is something we don’t talk about often enough,” Moore indicates. “There’s so much fear around cognitive health and even talking to a doctor about getting an assessment. I think it needs to be normalized.”.

To learn more about how you can be proactive for your brain health, visit BrainHealthMatters.com.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist.
  • A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.
  • In the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist. The Tiffany & Co. designer got his start in the 1930s with costume jewelry, crafting clips, buttons, and other accessories for Elsa Schiaparelli’s couture collections. “The way he came to jewelry was unpretentious: simple coats of paint on metallic works that looked shiny and lacquered,” says Sylvain Cordier, the Paul Mellon curator and head of the department of European art at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. “I’mconvinced that starting with costume jewelry very much informed a taste for bold colors.”.

A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.

In the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings. His first paillonné piece, the Croisillon bracelet, debuted in 1962. Philanthropist and Schlumberger devotee Bunny Mellon soon introduced her friend Jackie Kennedy to the style, which the first lady wore so often it became known as the “Jackie bangle.” Schlumberger also applied the enameling to earrings and decorative objects prized by collectors like Mellon, whose Schlumberger collection is held at the Virginia MFA.

Rings from the Enamel by Tiffany collection.

Tiffany, which recently revealed a collaboration with the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris to preserve Schlumberger’s archives, continues to honor the artistry of his paillonné pieces with its Enamel by Tiffany collection. The house, which employs some of the only remaining artisans skilled in the technique, is expanding these offerings this fall with newly introduced pieces that include rings and watches. Despite the decades that have passed since the Croisillon’s debut, Cordier still finds it to be fresh. “When you look at the Schlumberger pieces, there’s this sort of abstract effect,” he states. “I think it’s very modern.”.

Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health enhancement on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.
  • The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.
  • Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health enhancement on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

Industry observers note that “She came into my room and mentioned, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”.

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

Industry observers note that while MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

Recent findings suggest that “An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as upcoming evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”.

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:.

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

Sources indicate that “MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder remarked.

According to recent reports, “For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:.

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he remarked.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

Sources indicate that “MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder noted. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”.

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder remarked.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is crucial that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”.

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

According to recent reports, “A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

  • Service Recovery Update:Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it imposed after the record $6.4 billion hack of the exchange in October, four weeks after the attack.

"Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted," the exchange mentioned in an announcement on Thursday.

Service Recovery Update:Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted. Withdrawals are open across nearly all networks. Separately, a small number are temporarily paused due to network maintenance, which… pic.twitter.com/QZmXhsc2qA.

— Binance (@binance) November 26, 2026.

Withdrawals for a small number of networks are still temporarily paused while they undergo maintenance or planned upgrades, affecting a very small percentage of regular traffic, Binance noted. That is separate from its recovery work and part of its standard practice of pausing a network's withdrawals when external conditions require it, the exchange added.

Binance noted all user assets remain fully backed, and pointed users to its proof of reserves website, where they can check that their holdings are backed at least 1:1.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BNB with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The exchange also warned that events like the hack can attract phishing attempts. It stated it will never ask people for their passwords, two-factor authentication codes or seed phrases, and will never contact them to "speed up withdrawals," offer "priority processing," or move their assets into a "Binance vault.".

Industry observers note that the FBI has attributed the October 29 attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. North Korea has denied involvement. Binance set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses after the hack, and has won a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts.

According to recent reports, efforts to recover the stolen crypto are ongoing. On Monday, the U.S. Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture action for more than $1.1 billion in USDC stolen in the hack, and stated the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto since the attack.

The hackers have continued to move what they still control. More than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through cross-chain exchange THORChain, according to estimates from blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and Elliptic, Reuters reported. Elliptic told the news agency that $342 million has also moved through a Bitcoin coinjoin service, a technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, up from the $247 million it reported earlier this week.

Laundering the funds could take months or even years, but cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea, TRM Labs' global head of policy Ari Redbord told Reuters.

According to recent reports, the FBI on October 31 called on crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block addresses linked to the hack. THORChain, which says it does not censor transactions or carry out Know Your Customer checks, may have earned as much as $1 million in fees from the launderers' swaps, according to TRM Labs estimates cited by Reuters.

Sources indicate that why not just shut THORChain down after a hack?@CBarraford's answer to @RBoccius : by his count, 98% of THORChain's volume is legitimate trading. Shut it down and you hit all those people, the ones using it for their own financial freedom.

The hackers would barely notice.… pic.twitter.com/ax7Bwz9Uvu.

— THORChain (@THORChain) November 26, 2026.

Industry observers note that THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford defended the protocol in a video posted by THORChain on Thursday, saying that by his count 98% of its volume is legitimate trading. Shutting it down would hurt those who use the system for "completely neutral and good purposes for their own individual financial freedom and liberty," while barely inconveniencing the hackers, he argued. Bad actors will "find a way to get out just the same, they'll still go through Russian dark net things or Chinese," he remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that THERE ARE THINGS in your life that will change as you age. That's especially the case once you pass the half-century mark. After all the accumulated mileage of your 20s, 30s, and 40s, with the small nicks and scrapes that pile up over the years, those changes might be that you move a bit slower, or you don't bounce back as rapidly. This is totally normal. You might need to ease up on some aspects of your fitness practice—but you shouldn't be discouraged. You don't have to give up on your goals. You just need to reframe your approach, since you can still make gains after 50.

The key is to be smart—and smart training follows a initiative for longevity. You'll have just that with the super-popular MH MVP Premium Max Muscle at 50 program. Series creator Bryan Krahn, C.S.C.S. is a veteran trainer who knows what it takes to keep guys moving and healthy as they get older. He's his own proof of concept. He's in his 50s himself, and uses the same principles behind the program in his own workouts.

Follow the tips from Krahn below to continue building muscle and strength into your sixth decade on Earth and be sure to check out his entire Max Muscle at 50 workout program here.

Recent findings suggest that lifting heavy can be a young man's game. Krahn isn't saying that you should never pick up a big weight again—only that you can safeguard your joints by going lighter. You can still make gains this way, too. Krahn notes that studies suggest that you can still build muscle with higher rep rangers, up to 30 per set.

"Lighter weights will pack on size, as long as they make you work," he indicates. "So aim to use a weight that will push you when you're hitting 15 to 20 rep sets.".

Industry observers note that krahn wants you to know that the myth of the fragile over-50 guy is a load of bunk. He says you should be doing more, if anything, not less. The key is that you shouldn't be crushing yourself with every workout.

It has been revealed that his advice: Hit two or three hard training days per week. For the remainder of the time, stay active. Go on a run or walk, take a yoga class, or opt for your other favorite method of moving.

According to recent reports, you can still train hard and make gains, yes—but you need to remember that your body has accrued significant mileage, so there's bound to be some wear and tear. You'll have to make more adjustments in your routine than you did when you were younger to stay in the game, so don't be afraid to shift your schedule as needed.

According to recent reports, be smart and listen to your body. Take days off when you need them, and don't be afraid to swap out exercises when you're not feeling 100 percent with a particular movement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation.
  • Industry observers note that and that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise.
  • In a recent development, there are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

Industry observers note that and that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

In a recent development, there are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

Carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, says Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

Fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a substantial role in satiety, White says. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—important at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

Sources indicate that cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

Breaking: A Minimalist House in Italy Makes the Case for Less

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein.
  • Recent findings suggest that pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint.
  • Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Recent findings suggest that pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

A sauna is clad in blackened wood.

In a recent development, pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People remarked, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”.

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Sources indicate that ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother said, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”.

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface.

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth.

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”.

Sources indicate that at some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-proposal kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he states. Living in and feeling the house is key.

Smith-Petersen and Pawson on-site.

According to recent reports, the yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

The open-plan dining area and kitchen.

In a recent development, “Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia prepares to unveil a newly introduced EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.

It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV, created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.

Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.

In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.

“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia mentioned, the brand plans to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-latest B-segment EV hatchback.

It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a new dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.

Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the upcoming EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.

In a recent development, lee stated the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.

The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.

While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.

Industry observers note that as its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia said the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia aims to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.

The new EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.

It has been revealed that what will the EV1 look like? According to Auto Express, the entry-level EV will look a bit sportier and less boxy than the EV2 SUV. It could draw inspiration from the Vision Meta Turismo concept.

Sources indicate that it also apparently won’t be based on the Picanto, Kia’s smallest gas-powered car. The Kia EV1 is expected to bring a unique style to the family.

Recent findings suggest that this is good to see and makes sense, especially in Europe. I don't think Kia can go wrong making vehicles at so many different price points. It allows them to reach different segments and almost literally have something for almost everyone.

While all of Kia’s current EVs feature its ccNC infotainment system with dual 12.3″ instrument display and infotainment screens, plus a 5″ climate control panel, the EV1 could bring a simpler setup.

Like its other electric models, the EV1 is expected to receive the GT treatment. However, as an entry-level model, it may not use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup like the others.

Sources indicate that will Kia bring the EV1 to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Kia has previously mentioned the B-segment hatchback is designed for Europe. It could even be built alongside the EV2 at Kia’s plant in Slovakia.

The good news? The EV3, Kia’s compact electric SUV, is now on sale in the US, starting at just $29,890.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • THE HERD OF 400-pound caribou was running 50 miles an hour and directly at me.
  • It has been revealed that I could hear their breathing, smell their coats, and see all the details of their ornate antlers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE HERD OF 400-pound caribou was running 50 miles an hour and directly at me. The 30 animals had been eating lichen in the Arctic tundra in Alaska when something spooked them. I was sitting in their escape route. The ground began to vibrate once they cracked 100 yards. At 50 yards, I could see their hooves smashing the ground and kicking up moss and moisture. Then they were at 40 yards, then 35.

It has been revealed that I could hear their breathing, smell their coats, and see all the details of their ornate antlers. Just as I was wondering if the rescue plane would be able to spot my hoof-pocked corpse, one of the caribou noticed me and swerved. The herd followed, shaking the earth as they swept left and summited a hillcrest, their antlers black against a gold sky.

That moment when those caribou shook the earth also shook my soul. It was transcendent, wild as a religious experience. And it’s not even the most intense thing I did in Alaska. I experienced savage weather, crossed raging rivers, and faced a half-ton grizzly. My brain was feeling less hunkered down in its typical foxhole—a state I’d compare to that of a roadrunner on meth, dementedly zooming from one thing to the next. My mind felt more like it belonged to a monk after a month at a meditation retreat. I just felt . . . better. The biologist E. O. Wilson put what I was feeling this way: “Nature holds the key to our aesthetic, intellectual, cognitive, and even spiritual satisfaction.”.

When I returned from the wild, my Zen-like buzz hung around for months. To understand what was happening, I met with Rachel Hopman, Ph.D., a neuroscientist at Northeastern University. She told me about the nature pyramid. Think of it like the food pyramid, except that instead of recommending you eat this many servings of vegetables and this many of meat, it recommends the amount of time you should spend in nature to reduce stress and be healthier. Learn and live by the 20-5-3 rule.

Recent findings suggest that THAT’S THE AMOUNT of time you should spend outside in nature, like a neighborhood park, three times a week. Hopman led a new study that concluded that something as painless as a 20-minute stroll through a city botanical garden can boost cognition and memory as well as improve feelings of well-being. “But,” she said, “we found that people who used their cell phone on the walk saw none of those benefits.”.

Other research discovered that 20 minutes outside three times a week is the dose of nature that had the greatest effect on reducing an urban dweller’s levels of the stress hormone cortisol.

Sources indicate that in nature, our brains enter a mode called “soft fascination.” Hopman described it as a mindfulness-like state that restores and builds the resources you need to think, create, process information, and execute tasks. It’s mindfulness without the meditation. A short daily nature walk—or even a walk down a tree-lined street—is a great option for people who aren’t keen on sitting and focusing on their breath. But turn off your phone—alerts from it can kick you out of soft-fascination mode.

In a recent development, THE MINIMUM LENGTH of time each month you should spend in semi-wild nature, like a forested state park. “Spending more time in wilder spaces does seem to give you more benefits,” said Hopman.

According to recent reports, A 2005 survey conducted in Finland found that city dwellers felt better with at least five hours of nature a month, with benefits increasing at higher exposures. They were also more likely to be happier and less stressed in their everyday lives.

Recent findings suggest that the Finnish government then funded another study in 2014 in which the scientists dumped people in a city center, a city park, and a forested state park. The two parks felt more Zen than the city center. No shocker. Except that those walking in a state park had an edge over the city-park people. They felt even more relaxed and restored. The takeaway: The wilder the nature, the better.

Nature has these effects on the mind and body because it stimulates and soothes us in unusual and unique ways. For instance, in nature you are engulfed in fractals, suggested Hopman. Fractals are complex patterns that repeat over and over in different sizes and scales and make up the design of the universe. Think: trees (big branch to smaller branch to smaller branch and so on), river systems (big river to smaller river to stream and so on), mountain ranges, clouds, seashells. “Cities don’t have fractals,” mentioned Hopman. “Imagine a typical building. It’s usually flat, with right angles. It’s painted some dull color.” Fractals are organized chaos, which our brains apparently dig. In fact, scientists at the University of Oregon discovered that Jackson Pollock’s booze-and-jazz-fueled paintings are made up of fractals. This may explain why they speak to humans at such a core level.

Nature lifts us in other ways, too: Think smells and sounds. The feeling of the sun’s warm rays. Or just the fact that you’re getting out of the stress of your home or office. “It’s probably a mix of a lot of things,” said Hopman. Environments like cities, with their frenetic pace, right angles, loud noises, rotten smells, pinging phones, and to-do lists, don’t offer this.

THIS IS THE TOP OF THE PYRAMID. Three is the number of days you should spend each year off the grid in nature, camping or renting a cabin (with friends or solo). Think: places characterized by spotty cell reception and wild animals, away from the hustle and bustle.

This dose of the wildest nature is sort of like an extended meditation retreat. Except talking is allowed and there are no gurus. It causes your brain to ride alpha waves, the same waves that increase during meditation or when you lapse into a flow state. They can reset your thinking, boost creativity, tame burnout, and just make you feel better.

It has been revealed that this is likely why one study found that three days in the wild boosts creativity and problem-solving abilities and another found that U. S. military vets who spent four days white-water rafting were still buzzing off the wild a week later. Their PTSD symptoms and stress levels were down 29 and 21 percent, respectively. Their relationships, happiness, and general satisfaction with their lives all improved as well.

Industry observers note that when I returned from Alaska, my wife and I moved to the edge of the desert in Las Vegas. She wanted a shorter commute, and I wanted more access to nature. I now walk my dogs through red-rock trails for at least 20 minutes daily and on Sunday do a long trail run deep into the canyons to rack up my five-hour quota for the month. This summer, I’m planning a weeklong backcountry fly-fishing trip in Idaho’s Frank Church–River of No Return Wilderness Area. Hoping I’ll return less frazzled, fitter, and feeling more alive.

Michael Easter is a health and fitness writer, a visiting lecturer at UNLV, and the author of The Comfort Crisis.

Breaking: What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like all blockchain projects, Ethereum is under active development, with upgrades designed to make it faster, cheaper, and easier to use.
  • Instead of a single "Ethereum 2.0" event, the network upgrades through coordinated changes called hard forks that introduce new features or modify how the protocol operates.
  • Since the Merge in September 2022, developers have focused on scaling, lowering transaction costs, improving wallets, and making it easier to run nodes and validators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like all blockchain projects, Ethereum is under active development, with upgrades designed to make it faster, cheaper, and easier to use.

Instead of a single "Ethereum 2.0" event, the network upgrades through coordinated changes called hard forks that introduce new features or modify how the protocol operates.

Since the Merge in September 2022, developers have focused on scaling, lowering transaction costs, improving wallets, and making it easier to run nodes and validators. The Ethereum community is also aiming for roughly two major upgrades per year when research and testing are ready.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Industry observers note that ethereum's scaling initiative relies on layer-2 networks. These are separate blockchains built on top of Ethereum that process transactions off-chain and send results back to Ethereum for security and settlement.

Many layer-2 systems use rollups, which bundle multiple transactions together and post them to Ethereum as a single batch, allowing Ethereum to support more activity without the base chain processing every transaction.

It has been revealed that as a result, much of Ethereum's development has focused on making it cheaper and easier for rollups to use the network. More recent upgrades have also aimed to scale Ethereum's base layer directly, by raising the amount of activity each block can hold.

In July 2022, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin described the network's six roadmap phases as the Merge, the Surge, the Scourge, the Verge, the Purge, and the Splurge.

These phases are not single upgrades but broad goals, and several progress in parallel.

Ethereum's roadmap is implemented through a series of hard forks.

Glamsterdam is the upgrade after Fusaka, and its name combines "Amsterdam," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devconnect location, and "Gloas," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star. It focuses on scaling Ethereum's base layer, with two headline features:.

Sources indicate that glamsterdam also raises the gas cost of creating new state, such as accounts and contracts, to target database growth of about 120 GiB a year, and reprices reading stored data, to keep hardware requirements manageable as capacity rises. Under one proposal, EIP-8037, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as before.

Other scheduled changes would make a standard ETH transfer between existing accounts up to 71% cheaper, let developers deploy contracts to the same address across chains, make ETH transfers emit a log that apps can track, raise the maximum contract size from about 24KiB to 64KiB, and speed up validator exits and consolidations.

Node operators and stakers will need to patch their clients to support the fork; ETH holders do not need to do anything.

Developers originally targeted the first half of 2026. Glamsterdam went live on the Sepolia testnet in October 2026, but a fork on the Hoodi testnet planned for October 26, 2026, was postponed after security firm ChainSecurity warned that the upgrade's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existing smart contracts.

According to recent reports, in November 2026, developers rescheduled the Hoodi fork for December 15, 2026, and agreed to ship the gas changes unaltered. As of November 2026, no mainnet date had been set.

Hegotá is the upgrade planned to follow Glamsterdam. Its name combines "Bogotá," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devcon location, and "Heze," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star.

As of its October 2026 enhancement, ethereum.org expected Hegotá on mainnet in the second quarter of 2027, with a fork on the Sepolia testnet to come first, though no dates had been confirmed. Two changes are scheduled for inclusion.

The headliner, Fork-choice Enforced Inclusion Lists (FOCIL, EIP-7805), aims to strengthen censorship resistance by having a committee of validators propose lists of transactions that block builders must include, so that no single party can keep a valid transaction out of a block. Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would let each account set its own rules for what counts as a valid transaction, rather than relying on a single fixed signature scheme. That would bring features such as social recovery, spending limits, multiple approvals and gas sponsorship directly into the protocol, and let accounts adopt signature schemes designed to resist quantum computers.

Dozens of other proposals are being considered, but none are settled, and the rest of Hegotá's scope is still being decided. In November 2026, some developers argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, with a decision on Hegotá's full scope expected in December 2026. Forkcast tracks the live status of each proposal.

Upgrade names and scopes can change during development as proposals are refined before each hard fork.

Ethereum's roadmap continues to evolve as research progresses and upgrades are tested on devnets and testnets before mainnet deployment.

This article was updated in November 2026, and will be amended as as upcoming milestones are confirmed.

Latest Update: Should We All Be Seeing a Concierge Doctor?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, for as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered.
  • Over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, for as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered. But lately, many people have been opting for a membership-based system where they pay a monthly or annual fee for on-demand care. This concept is called concierge medicine.

Over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed. Between 2018 and 2023, the number of direct primary care and concierge practice sites grew by roughly 83 percent, per a 2025 study in Health Affairs. (But there are also concierge practices specific to gynecology, longevity medicine, and even emergency medicine.).

“Over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of frustrations that patients have had in terms of access to care, long wait times, lack of continuity of care,” says Jane Zhu, MD, a primary care provider and associate professor of medicine at Oregon Health and Science University, and author of the Health Affairs study. There’s a real need for faster, more on-demand medical care—and concierge medicine is one way that patients are getting that.

Industry observers note that membership prices vary, with some costing as little as $9 a month for on-demand urgent and primary care, and others costing as much as $45,000 a year for top-tier care (at-home doctor visits for urgent care, X-ray imaging from your bed, and even private jets on standby for medical evacuation while you’re traveling). If you don’t live in a major city, many of these programs offer telehealth services all over the country.

Industry observers note that so, what’s the catch? Ahead, read up on everything you need to know about concierge medicine, including the pros and cons, and who it’s right for.

The premise is simple: paying a membership fee unlocks extra attention and access to care from your doctor.

According to recent reports, at most traditional clinics and hospitals, the goal is for doctors to see as many patients a day as possible. (More visits equals more insurance claims and/or copays, which in turn makes money for the practice.) With concierge medicine, doctors don’t operate within this same construct. Instead, they make money from membership fees, which means they can still turn a profit with a much smaller pool of patients. When you schedule an appointment with a concierge doctor, you’re not competing with hundreds of other patients for a time slot in the same way you would for a traditional doctor.

According to recent reports, when Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai, worked in traditional medicine, she only got about 15 to 20 minutes for each patient visit. Now, she has the freedom to extend her visits to 45 to 60 minutes and form closer relationships with her patients. “I'm able to go into deeper discussions from a more holistic perspective and have a different type of conversation,” she states. Talking more in depth about sleep, nutrition, and lifestyle habits in general is key to helping her patients prevent illnesses in the first place—not just treat them when they come up.

Additionally, getting lab work done through concierge medicine may be a smoother process. While some traditional practices may have you drop by LabCorp to get your blood drawn, for example, many concierge practices will just do it on site, and even go beyond your average complete blood count for in-depth lipid, hormone, and genetic panels. But everything isn't always included in the membership, so check before they draw.

When you need a specialist outside of your concierge practice, they’ll often have health navigators—people whose job it is to schedule your appointments for you, facilitate communication between your providers, coordinate prescriptions, and run point on any insurance claims. Because the health care system can feel so fragmented and hard to understand, the health navigation piece is a major highlight for many patients, says Scott Braunstein, MD, an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care.

According to recent reports, regarding costs outside of the membership fee and bloodwork, every concierge practice is different. At Tia, for example, preventative care services like yearly physicals or vaccinations are usually covered by insurance, but diagnostic appointments often come with additional out-of-pocket fees. That means that if you come in for a UTI, sick visit, or complaint about a upcoming health problem, it’ll often result in an additional charge on the patient’s end. The average copay for these kinds of visits at Tia is between $15 and $75—not too different from a traditional doctor’s appointment. However, at a high-end program where you pay entirely out of pocket, the care is pretty all-inclusive.

Recent findings suggest that as of now, there isn’t enough data on concierge medicine to determine whether this model provides superior health outcomes for patients—like fewer hospitalizations or better chronic disease management—compared to traditional systems. That being mentioned, there is one undeniable factor that contributes to good health: regularly going to the doctor. A 2026 report by the health policy initiative Milbank Memorial Fund found that people with chronic illnesses who regularly see a primary care provider have lower rates of hospitalization and emergency room visits—and lower health care costs on the whole.

According to recent reports, however, in the U.S., about one-third of adults don’t have a usual source of primary care, per the report. Concierge medicine is one way to bridge this gap of primary care access, and give people an easy, on-demand way to take care of their health. Appointments are easier to schedule, can often be taken from your phone or computer, and the experience is designed to just be more enjoyable and convenient. “When we remove barriers for people accessing care, people are more likely to engage in their health. And when people are more likely to engage in their health, they have better health outcomes,” notes Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the vice president of In-Office Care at One Medical.

In a recent development, if you can get into these models of care, they seem to be beneficial for both the clinician and the patient. But the question remains: “What happens if you can't get into those models of care?” notes Dr. Zhu.

The number of clinicians practicing in membership-based clinics grew by 78 percent between 2018 and 2023, per the Health Affairs study. That means that more clinicians are leaving traditional medicine for this model—which could put pressure on an already-stretched-thin primary care system. If more clinicians leave the traditional system, it could become harder for the people who can’t pay for concierge medicine to access the traditional care they need. So while concierge medicine may help some people live healthier lives, it doesn’t yet fix the broader need for more primary care access in the United States, notes Dr. Zhu.

According to recent reports, the study also found that while concierge medicine providers are growing, the share of physicians actually declined, and the number of advanced practice providers—like nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants—increased. These advanced practice providers were more likely to be upcoming entrants to the workforce with no prior employer. So while there are still concierge providers with a career’s worth of experience, you might be more likely to get a newer provider with less experience if you opt for concierge medicine.

In a recent development, if you’re frustrated with a fragmented health system where you have to be the one to connect the dots between all of your doctors, concierge medicine could be a welcome reprieve. For instance, Dr. Harvey expects to see more and more patients with chronic illnesses opting for concierge models in the next couple of years. If you have a condition like PMOS, for example, you might be seeing five different specialists to deal with the symptoms: a dermatologist, endocrinologist, gynecologist, nutritionist, and a primary care provider.

In a recent development, with a concierge practice that specializes in convenient, wraparound care, you may be able to see multiple of these specialists all in one place, and have a health navigator or coach to help you coordinate appointments, says Dr. Bhuyan. When you’re dealing with complex medical conditions, or just finding yourself going to the doctor a lot for illnesses or infections, paying for extra time and access to your doctor might just make for a better experience.

The term “concierge” can make this form of care seem cost-prohibitive—and some services certainly are. That remarked, there are a few options with low membership fees that take insurance, including One Medical (starting at $9/month), Sesame Plus ($10.99/month), Tia Signature ($25-a-month membership, only available in some states) and Folx ($44/month).

If you’re using insurance, you’ll have to do your research to determine how much you’ll pay out of pocket. Popular services like Tia, Allara, Folx, and One Medical accept a wide variety of insurance looks, but specify that copays and other fees can vary blueprint by plan, just like at the regular doctor. If you’re not using insurance, these practices usually specify self-pay costs in addition to the membership fee depending on the visit or service type, and depending on the care you’re looking for, it could be a bargain.

Sources indicate that before committing to a membership anywhere, find out which services will and won’t be covered (like lab testing or imaging), and how easy it is to cancel said membership if you decide it’s not a fit, notes Dr. Bhuyan.

Sources indicate that A lot of times, you can also find local doctors practicing concierge-style medicine, and there are search tools like MDVIP or NextMD, which connect patients with a network of in-person concierge physicians all over the country. And if you can’t find one near you, there are plenty of large-scale telehealth services at your fingertips. Be sure to research the doctor beforehand to make sure that they’re legit, and that their expertise aligns with your goals, says Dr. Bhuyan.

Industry observers note that overall, health care is shifting more towards patients’ autonomy. They want to “decide how their health care dollars are spent, whether that's through HSA prepares or other means. They’re more empowered to choose the service that works for them,” says Dr. Braunstein. So, only you can decide if a concierge doctor is right for you (and your wallet!).

According to recent reports, meet the experts: Jane Zhu, MD, is a primary care provider and Associate Professor of Medicine at Oregon Health and Science University. Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, is a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai. Scott Braunstein, MD, is an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care. Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the Vice President of In-Office Care at One Medical, a membership-based in-person and telehealth clinic owned by Amazon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, health and Human Services Secretary Robert F.
  • Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.
  • A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In a recent development, in December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” stated Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

It has been revealed that “The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no newly introduced data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”.

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

According to recent reports, A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

Industry observers note that however, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the newly introduced approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

It has been revealed that the change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse stated.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”.

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse noted.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”.

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination initiative for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no fresh studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse noted.

Bob Hope at Home: 10 Photos of the Comic’s Life Behind the Curtain

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA.
  • Born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings.
  • Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA. “Sometimes I do my best to hide it, but I’ve got a real crush on America,” he wrote in his 1990 memoir, Don’t Shoot, It’s Only Me. “Nobody ever had a girl like her. Nobody ever gave me as much affection, as much honor, or as much real estate.”.

Born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings. His family had little money and moved often throughout his childhood. After he found success on stage and it came time to raise his own brood, Hope put down roots in California. Across Toluca Lake and Palm Springs, the star’s homes offered a place to escape the limelight, spend time with his wife and four kids, entertain very famous guests, and indulge in his love of golf.

Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.

Hope (bottom right) at the family estate in Cleveland. The comic’s parents William Henry Hope and Avis Townes Hope are on the porch in the background. Hope was 20 years old at the time of the picture.

Industry observers note that hope and his family moved from London to the United States when he was four. In this 1923 photo, he’s pictured with friends and members of the Hope clan at their Cleveland home. Because money was tight, the family took in boarders to supplement Hope’s father’s income, according to the Library of Congress. In his 1954 memoir, Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope recalls his early days in Cleveland. “The first place we lived by ourselves was Standiforth Court,” he wrote. “We were always on the move. We lived at 2029 Euclid. After that we moved behind the Cleveland Express barns…. It was a long walk between the barns and our house. And if we got home after dark, it was scary…. Next we lived at 1925 East 105th, then at 1913, then at 2029—all on Euclid. We didn’t move very far, only to bigger houses which had more room for roomers.”.

Hope and his wife Dolores at home in the 1940s.

Hope married Dolores DeFina in 1934, and the couple adopted their first child, a daughter named Linda, in 1939. That same year, the comic bought a five-acre former walnut grove in Los Angeles’s Toluca Lake neighborhood at 10346 Moorpark Street. He transformed the property into a lavish French Revival estate, featuring a 14,876-square-foot main house with eight bedrooms and eight bathrooms; a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guesthouse; a staff residence; and a pool.

Hope and his grandfather catch up over tea.

It has been revealed that in this 1943 photo, Hope is pictured at home with his “Grandpop.” As a young boy in London, Hope lived with his family in a house his grandfather had built. “Grandpop had built a row of houses in Eltham. We lived in one of them. They were put together like stone battleships,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. After moving to the United States, his grandfather went on to build churches in Cleveland and Detroit. Hope reunited with him during a return trip to England in 1939—the star’s first visit since moving across the pond as a child. He recalls the occasion in his memoir, writing that “It wasn’t until I went back to England in 1939 that I got to know [Grandpop]. It was the first time I’d been there since I was four. The English papers reported: ‘One-time shoeshine boy and ironmonger’s assistant comes home.’ The English are supposed to be conservative and not given to exaggeration, but they hooked one there. How could I have been a shoeshine boy or ironmonger’s assistant when I was only four when I left there?”.

Hope and family at home in the 1940s.

In a recent development, back in California, Hope and his wife continued to grow their family. They adopted three more children: Anthony, born in 1940, and twins William and Eleanora, born in 1946. In this circa 1940s photo, the family of six is pictured at home. In Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope reflects on the choice to adopt. “No matter how strongly I feel about the word ‘family,’ Dolores feels even more deeply about it,” he writes. “When we found out that she couldn’t bear children, she began to bend my ear about adoption.” They welcomed their children through The Cradle, an adoption agency in Evanston, Illinois. “Of the five thousand, four hundred and nine babies that The Cradle has placed, there are eight Cradle babies out here in Hollywood,” he continues. “The Hopes are proud to be Cradle parents. I wish I could really tell you what The Cradle means to me here in Hollywood, where all day long the talk is box-office and autographs and premieres and who’ll get the Oscar. ‘The town of make-believe,’ they call it, but don’t get the idea everything is make-believe in Hollywood. There's nothing make-believe about our children. They are real.”.

Hope enjoys some family time in the living room with Dolores and two of their children.

Hope’s Toluca Lake estate was more than a family retreat; it was also a gathering place for celebrities and politicians, including Bing Crosby and Richard Nixon. When the property went on the market for $27.5 million in 2013, listing agent Jade Mills said, “[Hope’s] daughter, Linda Hope, would often peek down the grand staircase to see who was coming. She once spoke to Lucie Arnaz and Maria Cooper about doing a book about watching celebrities come and go called ‘Seen From the Landing.’”.

The home was “always impressively staffed,” Mills continued. “A full-time cook, butler, estate manager, and two housekeepers manned the property on a daily basis, while additional staff was hired for large receptions.”.

Hope, Dolores, and their four kids pose at home in 1958.

Industry observers note that in this 1958 photo, Hope and the family pose for a photo on the stairs. In Have Tux, Will Travel, the comic gushes about his wife as a mother. “Dolores has a wise and loving touch with our children,” he writes. “I’m lost in admiration of the job she has done with them, and with the job she’s done with keeping me in line. A lot of children whose fathers are in show business grow up too precocious, too wise, too fresh, too unfunny. That’s not true of our four. Dolores sees to that. She also sees to it that they’re having a devout rearing.”.

The family is shown here opening Christmas presents in 1964.

In a recent development, hope was determined to give his children space at home. “When our kids began to grow up, we fixed up a play room for them and gave them rooms of their own,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. “While we were at it, Dolores and I decided to redo the whole house. We tore out one entire downstairs wall and put in glass, so no matter where we are, we can look out at the garden and enjoy the California sun—if it shows up.”.

It has been revealed that while his home workspace was connected to the residence, it was its own separate world. “My office adjoins my house,” he writes. “It’s a different project, separate and distinct from our house. In fact, it’s on a different property. It was put up (and is owned) by Hope Enterprises. But it’s handy. The people I want to see on business can walk in and out without disturbing anybody…. It’s a nice set-up.”.

Hope was an avid golfer in his free time.

It has been revealed that hope was an avid golfer and built a one-hole golf course at his home in Toluca Lake, where he’s pictured here in this 1990-era photo. He once even stated that he considered golf to be his real job. “Golf is my profession,” he said, per ESPN. “Entertainment is just a sideline. I tell jokes to pay my greens fees.” The outlet further reported that he played more than 2,000 courses all over the world and golfed with everyone from Crosby to Dwight Eisenhower and Bill Clinton. “I’ve played all over the world, which means there isn’t a country with a course in which I haven’t three-putted,” Hope said.

Hope and Dolores at home in Palm Springs.

While Toluca Lake served as the family’s primary residence, Hope’s most iconic home was arguably his Palm Springs estate, where he and Dolores are pictured here in 1991. Designed by famed architect John Lautner, the 24,000-square-foot estate featured 10 bedrooms, dramatic arches, and a statement curved roof. The futuristic design closely resembled a spaceship. Hope once joked, “Well, at least when they come down from Mars they’ll know where to go.”.

According to recent reports, the home’s construction, however, was plagued by setbacks. According to the Los Angeles Times, when building began in the early ’70s, the structure caught on fire and burned down. The project was subsequently delayed for five years, during which time the couple’s interior designer, Arthur Elrod, was killed in a car accident. Dolores then took over the design duties. Lautner’s protégé Helena Arahuete recalled Dolores’s vision: “She wanted everything very ornamented, very rich—you know, gold and pink and black and mirrors everywhere.” Inspired by her friends Walter and Leonore Annenberg’s home, which had a pink roof, Dolores requested that their curved roof be covered in pink terra-cotta gunite.

According to recent reports, in 1991, at his Palm Springs pad, Hope hosted “Bob Hope’s Yellow Ribbon Party,” a homecoming celebration for U.S. troops. The soiree included celebrity guest appearances by Brooke Shields, Patti LaBelle, Jimmy Stewart, and former President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty.

Hope died at home in Toluca Lake in 2003 at the age of 100. The estate remained in the family until Dolores’s death in 2011, after which it was listed for $50 million. LA businessman Ron Burkle purchased the star’s Palm Springs pad in 2016, and two years later, added Hope’s Toluca Lake residence to his real estate portfolio.
