💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear.
  • Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress.
  • Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear. Whether you're venturing deep into the backcountry or exploring a local trail, your pack will be strapped to your back for an extended period of time. It needs to be reliable, comfortable, durable, and offer the right storage and organization options to suit your style of hiking. Oh, and affordability is a nice-to-have, too.

Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress. Backpack technology isn't what it used to be when your grandpappy was hitting the trail. It's far better but also a lot more complicated. You'll need to understand frame types and nylon fabric densities and hydration system compatibilities and—well, you get the picture. It's all just a little more confusing than it needs to be. That's why our expert team put together this guide to the best hiking backpacks to help you find the perfect pack without breaking your back and the bank in the process.

Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s Osprey’s reimagining of the classic rucksack design. It’s rugged yet lightweight, with a 45-liter capacity that’s more than enough for most hikers on all but the longest multiday treks. I personally love the streamlined exterior that cinches down tight for maximum compression. Osprey’s AirScape back panel offers just-right cushioning, coupled with simple torso-length adjustability to fit a wide range of body shapes and sizes.

After months of testing, this has consistently proven to be my go-to pack for most hikes because everything about it just works. Plus, the price point hits the midrange sweet spot, ensuring it’s affordable enough for most, even for first-time hiking backpack buyers on a budget. Bonus: An attached rain cover is included.

Recent findings suggest that at just 12 liters and weighing only 390 grams, this pack is designed for ultra-efficient climbs and lightning-fast summit assaults. It's the daypack you grab when most other daypacks are too much. I found the simple organizational layout—one main compartment and two zippered pockets (one internal, one external)—made wrangling my day hiking essentials a breeze. Additional gear loops at the rear provide extra space for hanging anything you might need at the ready. The just-right back padding, removable hip belt, and ventilated mesh shoulder straps were extremely comfy for tackling daily summits in the White Mountains.

It's all made from recycled, eco-friendly materials that are Bluesign certified, with a PFC-free DWR treatment. The best part? It's among the most affordable brand-name speedpacks we'd recommend this year.

Read More: How We Pack Hiking Backpacks.

Like every Gregory pack I've tested in the last two decades, the Paragon 60 is durable, cleverly designed, and features smart organizational options. But I'm including it here mainly because it's so dang comfy to wear. It features a widely adjustable torso length and an airy mesh back panel that breathes well thanks to a design that's 90 percent air. The hip belt is equally adjustable, too, with dynamic panels that move independently of the frame. Translation: It's the most comfortable pack I tested this year, even after hundreds of miles of hiking with fairly heavy loads.

Bonus: The PFAS-free durable water-repellent (DWR) coating on the body, bottom, and pack lining means it's more eco-friendly, too.

Read More: Best Cold-Weather Hiking Gear.

According to recent reports, yeti’s first foray into the hardcore hiking backpack game comes on the heels of its recent acquisition of the Mystery Ranch brand. The Skala is a deft combination of Mystery Ranch’s legendary design prowess and Yeti’s built-to-survive-anything durability. The former’s RipZip opening is the star of this pack, providing instant access to its contents with a quick one-handed pull. The Skala features multiple adjustment points and a clever load distribution system that combine to ensure a perfect fit and all-day comfort on the trail.

It has been revealed that true to the Yeti brand, it's packed with premium, heavy-duty materials built to survive years of abuse. The only downsides? At 3.4 pounds, it’s heavier than many in this weight class. It’s also pricier than most of its competition. But if you’re a fan of Yeti and/or MR and don’t mind the “buy once, cry once” price point, this is definitely worth considering.

Read More: Yeti Skala Backpack Review.

It has been revealed that for an all-in-one solution—a backpack that moves effortlessly from your morning commute to the office to the trail and back again—Peak Design's upcoming Outdoor 25L pack delivers. The frameless, low-profile build is extremely comfy on and off the trail. The brand's signature organizational elements are here, too—it's hydration system-compatible, features a 16-inch laptop sleeve, and is purpose-built to accept PD's own gear cubes (sold separately) so you can divvy up the main compartment however you see fit. The drawstring/roll-top closure provides quick and easy access to the internal compartment while protecting your gear from the elements. Fair warning, though: You'll pay a premium for the PD brand name. If you’re looking to size up, the Outdoor Backpack is also available as a more generous 45-liter option.

In a recent development, mountain Hardwear is upending the ultralight backpacking game with the debut of the all-newly introduced Alakazam series. The 45-liter model won a coveted spot in this year’s Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. At just 820 grams, it’s absurdly lightweight with a trail-friendly fit that feels like wearing nothing at all. Yet, it offers enough room for both gear-heavy day hikes and overnights. It’s all thanks to the bleeding-edge ALUULA shell fabric, which is not only light but extremely durable. The storage and organization (with plenty of loops, pockets, and oversized stash pouches) are cleverly laid out, and the unique GiddyUp compression system allows you to cinch your load down on the go. I also especially love the roll-top design that makes the entire bag waterproof. (A 60-liter option is also available.).

Read More: Testing the Alakazam 45.

Like many Arc'teryx packs, the Alpha FL30 is first and foremost built for climbing (including a top strap, six lash points, and a built-in RECCO reflector for SAR situations). But, I also found its sleek silhouette and featherweight construction great for fast-packing. It's only as heavy as it needs to be while still protecting your gear with the brand's own abrasion-resistant Hadron grid fabric. The drawstring opening provides quick access to a cavernous, open-concept interior with only a single, small zippered security pocket.

It's a no-frills design with minimal organization options that won't please every hiker. But it's a solid, if pricey, option for hard-charging trail lovers who appreciate a pack that stays out of its own way.

With a 44-liter capacity, the Talon 44 is large enough for two-day weekender trips and even longer multiday treks. It's an ideal bag for most hikers looking to buy just one backpack that does it all. I love the slim profile, excellent padding, and close-to-body fit—all of which makes for more comfortable wear, especially after long days on the trail.

In a recent development, this iteration of Osprey's bestseller features a long list of upgrades to the straps, padding, and overall design. Plus, I found the sheer number of storage options to be perfect for almost any length of trip.

According to recent reports, I’ve been a fan of Gossamer Gear’s featherweight fastpacker-friendly gear for years. The Grit 28 is my go-to for fast day hikes and quick summit assaults where I’m willing to trade comfort and convenience for speed. At just over a pound, the 28-liter pack is streamlined and sized right. The storage options are limited, ensuring you pack only what you need and nothing more.

What sets it apart from most of its competition is the vest-style shoulder and sternum straps that wear more like a racing vest for maximum all-day comfort. Despite its light weight, it’s made from two ultra-durable fabrics that I’ve found stand up to plenty of trail abuse.

In a recent development, the Crossroads 27L Carry-On is, first and foremost, a travel backpack (it fits under most airline seats, making it a great carry-on backpack). But Yeti bakes in plenty of trail-ready durability to make this one good enough for hiking, too. The 700-denier TuffSkin Nylon exterior is both water- and abrasion-resistant, with an extra durable and easy-to-clean PU-coated base. Contoured, EVA-foam shoulder straps and a no-pressure back panel make for easy carrying, even during long layovers.

It has been revealed that plus, with a suspended laptop sleeve and multiple zippered pockets inside and out, this has become my go-to weekender bag, especially on trips where I'm intent on hitting the trail straight from the airport. (Pro tip: Pair it with Yeti's own Crossroads packing cubes for maximum organization options.).

Ultimately, every hiking backpack is designed for hauling "stuff." The amount of stuff each pack can carry—its capacity—is measured in liters (L) or cubic inches. The right size for you depends on how long you typically hike for (hours, days, weeks?) and how heavy a packer you are. If you're shopping for your first pack, finding the perfect capacity can involve a little trial and error. But for a wide variety of hikers, the following numbers are a good starting point.

If you tend to pack light, the right capacity for you may fall closer to the lower end of the above ranges. If you're an over-packer (no shame!), consider sizing up to a slightly larger pack with a capacity on the upper end of the above ranges. Again: Trial and error.

You may have heard an old hiker's adage that goes something like, "Ounces make pounds, and pounds make pain." It's a simple axiom, but it's true: The more weight you carry, the more work you need to do on the trail. That's why it's notable to pack as light as possible while still taking all the essentials. It helps to start with as light a hiking backpack as you can afford. The difference between three pounds and four pounds might not seem like much when you're standing in your living room, but I promise you'll feel every gram of that one-pound difference after 10 miles.

Sources indicate that there are three main types of backpack construction: internal frame, external frame, and frameless. External frame packs have largely been phased out in the mainstream outdoor gear space in favor of internal frame models. True to the name, they feature a rigid structure that's "hidden" inside the pack's back panel. They sit closer to the back, hugging the body for a more streamlined fit that's ultimately more comfortable. All but the smallest hiking backpacks we recommend below rely on an internal frame construction.

Industry observers note that some compact daypacks (usually 20 liters or less) use a frameless construction similar to standard school backpacks. The lack of a frame means they're not ideal for supporting heavier loads, but that typically isn't an issue if you're only carrying enough for an afternoon hike. Without a frame, most of these packs collapse down almost completely flat, making them perfect travel backpacks.

Sources indicate that some packs—particularly those designed for alpine climbers—rely on top-loading-only designs. Think of a typical shopping bag where the contents are only accessible directly through the top opening. It's simple but limiting. Thankfully, many of the best hiking backpacks these days are accessible via both top and side openings. For larger packs, this makes it infinitely easier to get to the gear at the bottom of your pack without having to take everything out first.

It has been revealed that the "best" storage layout is personal to each hiker. If you're an organizational nerd (I count myself among this camp), you may prefer more pockets to better wrangle your gear in a way that makes sense to you. On the other end of the spectrum are alpine-style bags that typically trade more pockets (and zippers and stitching) for a simpler, lighter-weight design. These tend to feature a single open-concept storage compartment with only one or two smaller storage pockets.

Industry observers note that A few pieces of gear you want to pack in your hiking backpack include: a hydration bladder, water bottle(s), a phone (with easy access to its camera), a satellite messenger, and bear spray. Most modern bags also offer external storage options, like reinforced crampon patches and gear loops or "daisy chains" (i.e., webbing stitched into the pack's exterior that provides multiple attachment points for wet gear, ice axes, helmets, and more that you may not want to store inside your pack).

Modern hiking backpacks can be deceptively complex, and there are dozens of technical features available on many of today's best models. If you're shopping for anything other than a daypack, consider a bag with a dedicated sleeping bag compartment and sleeping pad straps. For longer treks where you may want to venture away from base camp once you set up your tent, a removable daypack (sometimes the "brain" or top lid of a larger pack converts into an ultra-compact hip bag for this purpose), and a rain cover, which may be a stand-alone piece of fabric with a stretch seam or sewn into the pack itself, so you can easily pull it over the pack if the weather turns south.

As an outdoors writer, I spend countless weeks outside each year. During that time, I've put the most popular and well-reviewed hiking backpacks to the test to determine the best of the best. Over the last 12 months, I've tested dozens of packs from Mystery Ranch, Gossamer Gear, Gregory, Osprey, and more throughout the U.S., in Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Significant Bend National Park, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking backpacks, I've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, how well (or not) the weight is spread throughout, and how much gear can fit in them.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or a full-fledged expedition pack for tackling the wilds of Patagonia, we've got you covered with the 10 best hiking backpacks for any trail.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in Upcoming Jersey with his wife and their dog.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your upcoming favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered glitch, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

So when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

Industry observers note that the options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

It has been revealed that the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

According to recent reports, harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

It has been revealed that because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Industry observers note that opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Sources indicate that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

The idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he remarked, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

It has been revealed that in the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

It has been revealed that george Papanicolaou moved to Fresh York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

Sources indicate that his wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered fresh approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup stated in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

According to recent reports, “Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Industry observers note that instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen remarked this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

“This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

But does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” stated Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

According to recent reports, “Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he remarked. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over. A docuseries about the scandal, The Boy Who Stole Millions?, debuts on Prime Video November 30, and Netflix’s drama series The Altruists premiered November 19.

No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

The Orchid building at Albany, The Bahamas.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship. Bankman-Fried’s first crypto business was the quantitative trading firm he cofounded in 2017, Alameda Research. He went on to found crypto exchange FTX. Ellison, who first began working at Alameda in 2018, became its co-CEO and ran the firm as FTX’s hedge fund.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison moved to The Bahamas in 2021, reportedly motivated by looser COVID-19 pandemic protocols, and “a proactive stance taken by The Bahamas and its regulatory bodies on cryptocurrencies,” Bankman-Fried told Blockworks.

Recent findings suggest that the FTX and Alameda crews encamped at a luxury resort community called Albany. (Tiger Woods and Justin Timberlake are both investors.) Through his companies, Bankman-Fried purchased a penthouse in the sleek Orchid building there, named for its custom cutout façade. Designed by Morris Adjmi Architects, the Orchid’s blue latticework (inspired by New Orleans ironwork), is unmissable, offering an open-air feel to residents while signaling a layer of privacy to outsiders.

A reception area in the Orchid building.

Sources indicate that bankman-Fried shared his 11,500-square-foot unit with Ellison and eight other FTX and Alameda employees. The apartment has a circular living room, a light-up bar, Italian marble floors, cove lighting, and custom closets. Per a real estate listing obtained by Semafor, Bankman-Fried’s unit had German-engineered windows and doors. Outdoor amenities included a firepit, spa, grill and cooking area, and pool.

The couple attempted to evade culpability for misappropriating $8 billion of FTX customer money, a crime uncovered after Bankman-Fried bought his Bahamas property. Both were convicted of wire fraud and several conspiracy charges. Ellison served 14 months of a 24-month sentence. Bankman-Fried is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence and maintains that he is innocent.

According to recent reports, to bring this story to life for The Altruists, production designer Todd Fjelsted re-created the infamous penthouse. Several interiors were shot in Vancouver, but scenes requiring a beach or docks were shot in the Dominican Republic.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in a scene from The Altruists filmed in the Orchid set.

It has been revealed that fjelsted and his crew also built miniature replicas of real Albany buildings and a marina complete with a 10-foot remote-control yacht, using forced perspective to shoot them as backdrops. He calls this “the anti-AI set.”.

Industry observers note that in the dramatization, coworkers trade crypto in a communal office and party on a balcony overlooking the water. An employee in a hot tub bangs a gong for rounds of speed chess played on fancy sets. Inside, gaming is a major pastime, and there’s a baby grand piano on hand, though no one plays it. In real life, it was reported that Bankman-Fried kept a bean bag under the piano for napping.

Alex Lawther as Sam Trabucco and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

Industry observers note that looking to humanize the leads, Fjelsted observed how “insecurities [and] their feelings of a little bit of an imposter syndrome” informed Sam and Caroline’s design choices or lack thereof. Neutrals, sea colors, and palm tree prints made for a better on-camera look, but in real FBI interior photos, Fjelsted saw bedroom walls with powder blue sponge-painted over navy.

Garner and Boyle as Ellison and Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

Throughout the show’s eight episodes, the penthouse goes from bustling with the excitement of trading to vibrating with panic as the scandal comes crashing down. Eventually, the space is left nearly empty, with just Bankman-Fried and his parents remaining. In 2024, it was reported that Bankman-Fried’s real estate holdings would be sold off in order to pay back his debts, and today, the unit is indeed up for sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there.
  • After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J.
  • Recent findings suggest that his latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there. The 61-year-old director's work over four different decades includes the likes of Se7en, Fight Club, The Social Network, Gone Girl, and, now, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth; these are movies that know how to create a very specific style of tension that feels unique to a singularly talented visual storyteller, but are also entertaining thrillers that always have something to say. To put it simply, Fincher's films are often imitated, but never replicated.

After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz and his eventual blackballing from Hollywood for political reasons—got something of a tepid response (by David Fincher standards, at least), the director returned in 2023 with a movie far more in tune with what he's best known for in The Killer, which starred Michael Fassbender as a chilling contract killer who lives his life by a code in a world increasingly dominated by consumerism.

Recent findings suggest that his latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a kind of sequel to Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, reuniting Fincher with his most frequent leading man (in Brad Pitt) and allowing Pitt to reprise the character that won him his first Oscar for acting. There’s also the fact that the film features a script written by Quentin Tarantino, one that the Pulp Fiction director had originally planned to direct himself before his self-imposed ‘10 Films’ plan led him to abandon the project before Pitt and Fincher helped to revive it. (Fincher becomes the fourth person to direct a Tarantino script, joining a list that includes only Oliver Stone, Tony Scott, and Tarantino himself.).

Sources indicate that the movie shifts Tarantino’s bright, psychedelic ‘60s vibe of Hollywood for a darker, grittier one in the ‘70s that feels in line with Fincher’s whole thing. This is kind of a hangout movie, kind of a fixer movie, and kind of a neo-noir; it’s also a deeper exploration of Booth’s character and a real showcase for both Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan as a pair of fresh characters in show business.

It has been revealed that these are the kinds of conflicting, overlapping themes always present in Fincher's films, and part of what makes them so compelling. Fight Club, for example, is a satire on the kind of toxic masculinity that tends to make some people out there, well, the worst people in the world. Fincher himself has remarked that it's not his fault that some people tend to take the movie the wrong way, and we tend to land on his side. Time to work on that media literacy, clones.

We'd be remiss, too, to not talk about one of the collaborations that makes Fincher's more recent work pop so much: the presence of composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross. The Nine Inch Nails founder and his longtime collaborator have reinvented themselves in the past decade-plus as a constant presence in the industry, and their synths and tones make all of their work pop—but it feels especially right when paired with the visuals and performances that Mr. Fincher brings to the screen. That One Scene in Gone Girl (you know the one) is made even more memorable because of the music playing underneath, and the score for The Social Network is one of the best albums of the last 20 years.

That's enough for now, though. As you get ready for The Killer—or if you want to dive into Fincher's work all over again—we've got a complete ranking of all 13 feature films he's made in his impressive career.

According to recent reports, well, it’s no big surprise what’s at the bottom. Fincher has loudly disowned Alien 3, considered by many to be a low-point in an otherwise enjoyable franchise. To Fincher’s credit, it was his directorial debut and one where he was arguably set up to fail. As Ridley Scott was unavailable, the Alien 3 team cycled through multiple scripts and directors in a frantic attempt to recreate the success of the previous films. While Alien 3 has in more recent years been reconsidered by some fans to be at least a decent entry in the franchise, it’s without a doubt a notable stain on Fincher’s otherwise solid filmography. –Milan Polk.

The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008).

Loosely based on an F. Scott Fitzgerald short story, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button is a strange film to say the least. While the Oscar-winning film had great visual effects for its time, the film ultimately falls flat. While many great films have spawned from short stories, it’s clear that this particular story didn’t necessarily require more examination. It’s a hard sell to craft a thrilling romance out of the tragic and horrific tale of a constantly de-aging man. While at the time the film earned critical acclaim, it probably isn’t worth a rewatch. –MP.

It has been revealed that jodie Foster and Kristen Stewart as a mother and daughter duo? Sign us up. Panic Room is a solid thriller about a mother fighting for survival when three robbers come to steal the previous homeowners' bonds. It’s a perfectly watchable movie, but it’s not Fincher’s best. Released in 2002, Fincher was on a hot streak, coming off of Se7en, The Game, and Fight Club. After showing audiences some of his best work to date, it’s no wonder Panic Room didn’t land as strongly with its standard home invasion tale. Still, if anyone can make a decent thriller amongst his more well-known works, it’s David Fincher. –MP.

Mindhunter fans may have strong thoughts about Mank, which directed Fincher’s attention away from his Netflix series (although Fincher has said audience numbers and his own heavy involvement, which ultimately took a toll on him, were factors in its end). That said, Fincher’s first Netflix feature film was a passion project for the director, whose own father wrote a screenplay for the movie. While the film garnered 10 Oscar nominations–winning Best Production Design and Best Cinematography–it’s overall less compelling than Fincher’s other works. –MP.

Industry observers note that the Game isn't the most iconic Michael Douglas movie of the '90s—that honor probably goes to Basic Instinct. The Game isn't the most iconic David Fincher movie of the '90s either—well, just keep reading the rest of this list for a few more of those. But you know what The Game is? A damn fine movie, a thriller with a plot filled with twists that will keep you guessing and compelling from the very start to the final frame. The movie may actually border on a twist or two too many, but that's a critique we're happy to deal with. —Evan Romano.

Fincher's latest finds the director returning to his roots—tense thriller—in an entirely fresh way. Michael Fassbender plays the titular character in a story that's both intentionally dry and has something real to say about the ever-present state of consumerism in modern times—even for a methodical master assassin. It might take a bit to get fully into The Killer's trance, but once it kicks in, the hypnosis is very real. —ER.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

This movie existing at all is the kind of thing that movie lovers used to dream up as part of games invented to kill time. Fincher directing a script by Quentin Tarantino? Starring Brad Pitt? Like, yes please. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth has a story that feels like one of those pulp paperbacks you pick up before a long flight and can’t put down until you’re done (and given how much Tarantino has always loved the work of Elmore Leonard, that makes sense). It’s different from Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, and that’s OK—the vibe is different, and it’s endlessly compelling. Elizabeth Debicki, who plays a character who may or may not have been the titular character of Tarantino’s original project, is a real standout here. In short? It’s just fun.

The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011).

Sources indicate that just like with Gone Girl (which we'll talk about a bit later), The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo proves that Mr. Fincher does well with turning popular books into a visual medium. Steig Larsson’s posthumously published Millenium series found critical acclaim worldwide, so it was only right a great director took on the gritty, dark adaptation. In creating the film, Fincher faced multiple obstacles, including: Sweden released its own trilogy of films in 2009, and the Millenium series entries are all door stopper novels. That’s not to mention the book’s depiction of graphic violence, likely to turn away some audiences. Despite it all, Fincher crafted a solid adaptation. Rooney Mara and Daniel Craig each give stellar performances as the two protagonists, and the film does well to recreate the book’s overall moodiness. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo’s lower ranking isn’t due to its quality, but simply that Fincher’s filmography contains so much incredible work that they can’t all be in the top 5. –MP.

Sources indicate that for as significant as the true crime genre has gotten in recent years, nothing has managed to top Zodiac, Fincher's 3-hour epic telling of the saga that surrounded the Bay Area's infamous Zodiac Killer. The cast, led by fantastic performances by Jake Gyllenhaal, Mark Ruffalo, and Robert Downey Jr. (with great appearances from John Carroll Lynch and Brian Cox too), is actually only the second best part of the movie; the sense of constant dread that Fincher creates is both crushing for the viewer and extremely accurate to how it must have felt with one of American history's most horrific monsters on the loose. —ER.

It has been revealed that it's hard to find a movie more iconic than Fight Club. As one of many films released in 1999 to make a major cultural mark (think The Matrix, Being John Malkovich, The Sixth Sense, and The Blair Witch Project, among others), Fight Club is probably remembered most for its twist (which, if you somehow haven't seen the movie yet, we won't spoil here), and Brad Pitt's utterly unforgettable turn as Tyler Durden (along with an accordingly ripped body and stylish outfits). But even deeper here is a piece of work that puts Fincher's very best talents on full display: the movie is intense when it needs to be, very funny when it needs to be, and features some of the most memorable shots you'll see. Look folks, no one enters a room like Marla Singer. —ER.

Is Se7en a thriller? A mystery? A psychological horror? The answer to all of the above is a resounding Yes. All of the above. And it's absolutely masterful at all of it. After a rough experience on Alien³, Fincher hunkered down and made one of the all-time greatest movies of its kind. Led by a pair of commanding lead performances from Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman (as detectives investigating a series of grisly murders that seemingly follow a pattern inspired by the seven deadly sins), Se7en is dark, scary, and moody in a way that so many other movies in this world try to be—and can never quite pull off. —ER.

As you can see, The Social Network is not the #1 movie on our list. But we'd be hard-pressed to say it's not the single most impressive in David Fincher's one-of-a-kind filmography. Here, Fincher manages to turn a story unlike any he'd done before—the story of the formation and early years of Facebook contains absolutely zero elements of the crime thrillers he's most known for—into one of the most compelling dramas you'll ever see, with stunning photography and characters you can't look away from. This may be the best (and, in a way, most notable) movie of the 2010s, and I genuinely sometimes lose sleep when I remember that Fincher didn't win the Oscar for Best Director. —ER.

Trust David Fincher to bring out the best performance in Ben Affleck’s entire film career (yeah, we’re calling it: it’s the best).

As a major literary bestseller, Gone Girl was always going to be a thrilling movie adaptation. But with a director like Fincher, the film was not only a sensational thriller but an artistic work all on its own. It expertly captures the backdrop of post-recession millennial suburban malaise while chronicling a fascinating mystery. Rosamund Pike shines as the enigmatic and volatile Amy Dunne, rightfully earning herself a Best Actress nomination at the Academy Awards. Gone Girl is Fincher at his best, mixing his thriller skills with an astute exploration of contemporary culture, and a bit of his signature dark, dry, humor mixed in for good measure. If there’s any Fincher film that’s an absolute must-watch, it’s Gone Girl. –MP.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii.
  • Industry observers note that black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November.
  • Recent findings suggest that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Industry observers note that black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

Recent findings suggest that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

According to recent reports, wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most crucial tools for success.

Sources indicate that keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a strategy that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here.

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

In a recent development, equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Sources indicate that alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

In a recent development, why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 or 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this upper-body movement. “This exercise is so beneficial because you are working in a hinged position and teaching your body how to properly brace,” Harvey notes. “This will come in handy the next time you need to bend over and pick something up.”.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Why it rocks: This move strengthens your lower body while also improving stability, and the resistance band is great for added intensity.

Why it rocks: This beginner-friendly move works your glutes, core, and lower back, and may help mitigate back discomfort due to sitting.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges work the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, all while improving coordination and stability.

Sources indicate that strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

According to recent reports, “The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” states Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”.

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” claims Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

In a recent development, programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

In a recent development, “You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an matter trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

Recent findings suggest that A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

Industry observers note that to know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Industry observers note that the best exercise initiative is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” states Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”.

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) pilot that will let select Southern California Edison (SCE) customers send electricity from their EV batteries back to the grid. Eligible drivers could get more than $16,000 in help with equipment and installation, and earn money when the grid needs their power.

Industry observers note that GM says the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes. Through the California Energy Commission, eligible customers in SCE’s Emergency Load Reduction Program can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system and up to $8,099 toward eligible installation costs, including connecting the system to the grid.

In a recent development, chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV drivers can use time-of-use energy management to take advantage of lower rates and may be paid for participating in eligible demand-response events. How much they save or earn depends on their rate blueprint, electricity use, and participation.

GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities, and each program varies by utility.

Industry observers note that an EV battery stores direct current (DC), and your house and the grid use alternating current (AC). GM’s current home backup system uses a wall-mounted inverter to convert the power. With AC bidirectional charging, the car’s onboard inverter does the job. Moving that work into the car could make the equipment on your garage wall simpler and cheaper to install.

Not in CA, but we use solar, time of use, and EVs to minimize our energy costs. We’re not feeding power back to the grid from our cars, but the combo of TOU, solar and EVs does allow us to reduce costs significantly. Solar covers all the expensive peak power, I have the cars start charging early enough to use any extra solar, and the rest is off peak at half cost.

Industry observers note that GM is joining CharIN‘s North American AC V2G task force, which is working to align technical standards, equipment certification, and utility approval requirements. In Southern California, the pilot will give GM and its partners a look at how the process works for drivers, from signing up and getting the hardware installed to getting utility approval and sending power back.

Breaking: The Part of Your Holiday Hangover You Can’t See

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together.
  • According to recent reports, the liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more.
  • WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FOUR GLASSES OF wine? Your liver drinks them, too. Extra gravy? Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together. Nearly every bite you eat and every drink you down ends up getting managed by the same organ in your body: your liver.

According to recent reports, the liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more. But come the holidays, all the food and festive drinking can put your body’s largest organ to the test. Here’s how the wreckage happens and how to avoid accumulating long-term damage.

WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale. The liver also holds on to anything it can use, such as the antioxidants in wine or the carbs in beer. But that doesn’t mean alcohol is nutritious. Metabolizing alcohol also creates fatty acids along the way, which get stored as triglycerides—a kind of cholesterol—until your body can use them up. Typically, if you eat and drink moderately, your body processes them just fine. Until you...

THE MORE YOU drink, the more your liver shuffles those triglycerides into the “burn later” pile...until the pile is so massive that your liver can’t get to the bottom of it.

“If you binge, then binge again, then binge again, your liver gets shocked each time and can’t recover,” says Christopher Koh, MD, clinical director at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

Sources indicate that you may not feel the damage on your liver after the holiday or the next one. But over time, the holidays may overwhelm the organ. This can look like increased inflammation that eventually kills off liver cells, leaving scar tissue in their place (and can lead to cirrhosis, a problem in which 25- to 34-year-olds have the highest risk of death compared with other age groups). Not good. Experts say just three get-togethers a week through the holiday season can initiate inflammation if each outing involves more than five servings of alcohol in two hours. Not to mention when...

YOU DON’T EVEN have to drink alcohol to mess up your liver. Seasonal foods (you know the sides that are delicious but are high in saturated fat or refined carbs, along with processed red meat) combined with holiday-associated weight gain may increase the risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

“It’s estimated that up to 30 percent of the US population has [MASLD], and there aren’t symptoms, so people usually don’t know and aren’t doing anything to reverse it,” states Mazen Noureddin, MD, hepatologist at Houston Methodist.

Sources indicate that as obesity continues to rise, researchers estimate MASLD rates will rise to over 41 percent of the US population in 2050. That fat is wreaking the same havoc alcohol does—causing inflammation and eventual scarring—without the libations. MASLD may develop in as little as six weeks if you really overdo it.

YOU DON’T NEED to buy an activated-charcoal smoothie or a beet-juice detox cleanse to do it. Your liver can regenerate and naturally get itself back in working order if you move the heck out of its way. A month or so without a drop of alcohol (no beer during the game, no wine during date night) can reduce the fat storage in the liver and help tame inflammation. You can also undo some of the fat that causes MASLD by cleaning up your diet and cutting portion sizes: Losing 5 percent of your weight can reduce up to 25 percent of liver fat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

In a recent development, korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with newly introduced tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Recent findings suggest that days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

Sources indicate that in the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin swiftly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be fresh concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an vital role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

It has been revealed that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

But even so, a couch is the sort of thing you want to try before you buy. With the opening of a new flagship showroom in New York City's SoHo neighborhood, the brand is hoping you'll make a day of it; get comfortable, stay a while.

This month, 7th Avenue cut the ribbon on a 3,240-square-foot storefront in a historic cast-iron building at 476 Broome Street. It's the 30th brick-and-mortar space in the US and first permanent location in NYC to open since the brand's founding as a direct-to-consumer business in 2022. Co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw says that he and co-founder Josh Stinson decided to put down roots in the Significant Apple after seeing the way Fresh Yorkers took to their hero product—the "World's Greatest Modular Sofa," they call it—during the years they operated a pop-up shop in the city.

“The main showroom celebrates volume and openness, with soaring ceilings, dramatic columns, and refined architectural detailing,” notes Stinson.

Sources indicate that co-founders Stinson and Shaw sourced design details for the showroom from around the world. “[These items] have an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas,” indicates Shaw.

Industry observers note that "We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult," Shaw says. (The brand famously uses water-repellent and stain-resistant performance fabrics, and all sofa covers can be removed and thrown in the washing machine for cleaning.) Newly introduced Yorkers appreciated the modular designs, which can fit into petite elevators and through the narrow doors and hallways ubiquitous in city homes (gotta love a pre-war building!). “Our sofas arrive in individual boxes, making those tight spaces easier to navigate,” he adds.

According to recent reports, A store in Upcoming York was a no-brainer, but that doesn't mean finding a location was easy. Shaw and Stinson, who is COO, considered addresses in the Flatiron District, where shoppers can bop in and out of home retailers—like Herman Miller, Design Within Reach, ABC Carpet & Home, Crate & Barrel, the list goes on—without leaving a three-block radius. But ultimately they couldn't let go of SoHo's "unmatched" energy. "We wanted to find a place that is grand and historic, paying homage to NYC’s architectural heritage," states Stinson. With 14-foot ceilings and a skylight, "the space on Broome Street creates a sense of openness and grandeur from the moment customers walk through the door.".

Just how durable are 7th Avenue's furniture pieces? During the SoHo store's opening party, guests were encouraged to drop their drinks on the sofas in a “spill lab.”.

It has been revealed that shaw and Stinson, who designed the space themselves, say they used the building's architecture to create different vignettes and experiences for guests. The main showroom, for instance, with its dramatic columns and open space, is perfect for showing off 7th Avenue's larger sectionals. Elsewhere, a daybed is nestled into an alcove for a more intimate scene. "We wanted to demonstrate that great furniture design isn't simply about size," claims Stinson. "It's about proportion and the relationship between a piece and the space surrounding it.".

The two also wanted to show that "beautiful design should work for real life." "That meant balancing the stateliness of the cast-iron architecture and high ceilings with warm materials, organic textures, and comfortable places to sit," states Shaw.

Sources indicate that A light and bright backdrop of European oak and Turkish travertine is dotted with treasures gathered from around the world: coral stone coffee tables quarried from volcanic islands in Indonesia, century-old olive oil jars from Turkey and Morocco, sculptural plants like a Hawaiian dragon tree. "A Queensland Bottle Tree Bonsai, native to Australia and sourced from Los Angeles plant specialists The Plant Daddies, was shaped over two years to achieve its distinctive curved form," states Stinson. These details, Shaw adds, have "an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas.".

Guests readily settled into 7th Avenue's plush sofas at the flagship's opening party.

"We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," claims Stinson. At the opening party, props scattered about the furniture brought this idea to life.

Recent findings suggest that for all the finery, 476 Broome Street feels more like someone's home than an art gallery—and that's very on purpose. "We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," states Stinson. The co-founders want visitors to interact with the furniture. Indeed, a cheeky neon sign that reads "Come Spill on Me" hangs over an emerald velvet couch; at the store's opening party, red wine was passed with nonchalance and guests were invited to plop onto a double-wide sofa and pose for photos with an artful disarray of newspapers, a pizza box, and an overturned gag martini glass—no need to take their shoes off.

Sources indicate that according to Shaw and Stinson, great design should accommodate the realities of modern life, messy things like kids, pets, and parties. "Our clients appreciate beautiful, thoughtfully designed spaces, but they also want to live in them without hesitation," indicates Shaw. "Ultimately, we feel that luxury should be lived in, not simply admired.".
